passage: "Again English?" said Pankaj, his older brother, looking at the desk. "Since Sunday you have done English and Biology revision and nothing else." Kishore shrugged. "They feel good. I get them right." "What about Maths? The unit test is on Friday." "Later." "Later has been last month, Kishore." Kishore pushed his chair back. "In English I get nine out of ten. In Maths I sit and stare." Pankaj pointed at the report card. "English went up two marks. Maths went down, and it counts the same as everything else. Your total is stuck." Kishore looked at the numbers for a long moment. "I know," he said quietly, and closed the English book.

qa.q: Which two subjects had Kishore been revising?
qa.a: Kishore had been revising English and Biology.

qa.q: Why does Kishore keep revising English and Biology, and what does he feel about Maths?
qa.a: Because they feel good and he gets them right, while in Maths he just stares, so he avoids it, probably out of discouragement.

qa.q: What could Kishore do about Maths?
qa.a: Start with ten minutes of the easiest questions daily, because small wins make the subject less frightening.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel about Kishore's routine?
qa.a: Concerned, since he pointed at the report card and said the total is stuck.

grounding: A student keeps revising favourite subjects while Maths is skipped, so strong subjects rise slightly and the failing one drags the result.

subtype: Approach: avoidance by studying favourite subjects [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Irawati, and last term I was very busy avoiding Maths. Every evening I'd sit down meaning to do algebra and somehow end up making beautiful Biology flowcharts or rereading my English poems, because those felt good. I'd finish a Biology chapter and feel clever. Algebra just made me feel stupid, so I kept it for "later". Yusuf, who sits next to me, asked twice if I wanted to practise sums together. I said I was busy. Then the half-yearly results came. English up from 78 to 82, Biology up from 80 to 84. Maths: 29. My overall percentage actually fell, and Ma's face when she read the card still makes my stomach twist. Four extra marks in Biology don't carry a failing subject.

qa.q: What was Irawati's Maths mark in the half-yearly results?
Why did Irawati keep choosing Biology and English?
qa.a: Those subjects made Irawati feel clever and good, while algebra brought a feeling of being stupid, so avoiding it was a way to escape that discomfort.

qa.q: What would you change first in Irawati's evenings?
qa.a: Start each evening with a short, fixed slot of Maths, perhaps with Yusuf, before any favourite subject, so the hard part gets the freshest time.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt when Irawati said they were busy?
qa.a: Yusuf may have felt a little brushed off, having twice offered help that could have made the Maths easier.

grounding: A student looks back on revising favourite subjects while skipping Maths, and the failing subject dragging down the result.

subtype: Approach: avoidance by studying favourite subjects [Pitfall]
passage:
Class teacher's note after the parent meeting, 14 October — Ayesha, Class 11
Ayesha's mother told me Ayesha studies "for hours every night". That matches what I see: her Economics and English notebooks are the neatest in the class, and both marks went up a little this term. Accounts is a different story. Her Accounts notebook has almost nothing after the first chapter, and she scored 22 out of 80 in the unit test, which pulled her overall grade down again. When I asked, she said quietly, "I'll do Accounts once the others are sorted." I think the others feel safe and Accounts feels like failing. I have paired her with a classmate for Accounts in the library on Wednesdays, and asked her mother to make sure Accounts comes first each evening, not last.
— Sunaina

qa.q: What did Ayesha score in the Accounts unit test?
What might Ayesha be feeling when she says she'll do Accounts later?
qa.a: She is probably anxious and embarrassed about Accounts, so her safe subjects give relief from the feeling of failing.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Ayesha better, and why?
qa.a: Doing Accounts first each evening, with support like the library pairing, because the subject dragging her grade needs the freshest time, not the leftovers.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's mother see the long study hours now?
qa.a: Ayesha's mother may be surprised and worried to learn that the hours went to the safe subjects while Accounts was left behind.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a student polishing strong subjects while skipping Accounts, which keeps pulling the overall grade down.
